title: The NFL: America's Biggest Game
subtitle: How American football works, and the moments and players that made the league famous.
description: A B1 reading and listening text on the National Football League: the basic rules, three famous plays, and the players Americans still argue about. With vocabulary, comprehension and discussion practice.
passage: The National Football League, or NFL, is the top professional American football league, and for many Americans it is far more than a sport. Games fill stadiums on autumn weekends, the Super Bowl is one of the most-watched television events of the year, and many families treat game day as a social occasion built around food and friends.

The league has 32 teams, split into two conferences: the National Football Conference (NFC) and the American Football Conference (AFC). Each conference is divided into four divisions. In the regular season, every team plays 17 games across 18 weeks, which means each team gets one week off, called a bye week. Fourteen teams then reach the playoffs, seven from each conference, and those playoffs end with the Super Bowl.

The game itself looks complicated, but the basic idea is simple. Two teams of eleven players are on the field at a time. A team scores by carrying or throwing the ball into the other team's end zone for a touchdown, or by kicking the ball between the uprights for a field goal. The team with the ball gets four attempts, called downs, to move it at least ten yards. If they succeed, they get another four downs and keep going. If they fail, the other team takes over.

Some plays have become part of American sporting memory. In 1972, in a game now known for the "Immaculate Reception", the Pittsburgh Steelers running back Franco Harris caught a pass that had bounced off another player and ran it into the end zone. It won the game and gave the Steelers their first playoff victory.

In Super Bowl XLII, the New York Giants receiver David Tyree made what fans simply call "the helmet catch". Closely covered by Rodney Harrison of the New England Patriots, Tyree trapped the ball against his own helmet and held on. The catch led to a touchdown and helped the Giants win a game almost nobody expected them to win.

Super Bowl LI produced the greatest comeback the game has seen. The New England Patriots were 25 points behind the Atlanta Falcons, and they still won, in overtime. For a lot of fans, that night is the clearest example of why they keep watching until the end.

The league has also produced players people still compare and argue about. Jerry Rice, a wide receiver, caught more passes for more yards than anyone in NFL history. Walter Payton was a famously powerful runner and held the all-time rushing record for years, until Emmitt Smith passed him in 2002.

At quarterback, the position that usually decides games, three names come up again and again: Joe Montana, who stayed calm in enormous moments; Tom Brady, who won more Super Bowls than any other player; and Peyton Manning, who was known for reading a defense almost like a coach. On defense, the linebacker Lawrence Taylor changed how the position was played, combining speed and strength in a way offenses had not had to deal with before.

From a small league in the 1920s to a global business today, the NFL has kept its hold on American attention. You do not have to follow it closely to notice it, because in the United States the season, the rivalries and the Super Bowl are part of the calendar.

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: These questions do not repeat the words of the text. Work out the answer from what it means.

items.prompt: The league is split into two conferences, and each conference has four divisions. How many divisions are there altogether?
items.explanation: Two conferences with four divisions each gives eight. The text gives you the two numbers separately and expects you to put them together.

items.prompt: Every team plays 17 games, but the season runs for 18 weeks. What does that difference mean for a team?
options: It plays twice in one week
It has one week with no game
It plays one game in the playoffs
items.explanation: One more week than games means one week off — which is what the text calls a bye week.

items.prompt: A team has used all four of its downs and moved the ball only six yards. What happens next?
options: The opposing team gets the ball
It must kick a field goal
items.explanation: Ten yards are needed to earn a new set of downs. Six is not enough, so, as the text puts it, “the other team takes over”.

items.prompt: Why does the text call the 1972 catch remarkable?
options: Harris caught a ball that had already bounced off another player
Harris ran the length of the field
Harris caught the ball against his helmet
items.explanation: The ball was deflected before he caught it, which is what made it extraordinary. The helmet catch was a different play, thirty-six years later.

items.prompt: What do the helmet catch and the Super Bowl LI comeback have in common, according to the text?
options: Both involved the New England Patriots winning
Both produced a result almost nobody expected
items.explanation: The Giants won “a game almost nobody expected them to win”, and the Patriots won from 25 points behind. Note that the Patriots lost the first of those two games.

items.prompt: Why is Walter Payton no longer the all-time rushing leader?
options: Another running back overtook his total in 2002
He retired before he could set the record
Jerry Rice gained more yards than he did
items.explanation: Payton held it “for years, until Emmitt Smith passed him in 2002”. Rice's records are for receiving, a different thing entirely.

items.prompt: The text says Peyton Manning read a defense “almost like a coach”. What does that suggest he was good at?
options: Throwing the ball a long way
Understanding what the other team was about to do
items.explanation: Reading a defense means working out its intentions in advance — a thinking skill, not a physical one.

items.prompt: Why does the text say you do not have to follow the NFL closely to notice it?
options: Because the games are shown everywhere for free
Because the season, the rivalries and the Super Bowl are part of the American calendar
items.explanation: The final sentence makes that point: the sport is embedded in the shared calendar, so it reaches people who do not follow it.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement is true, based on what the text means — the wording is not the same.

items.statement: The Super Bowl is the last game of the season.
items.explanation: True. The text says the playoffs “end with the Super Bowl”, which is another way of saying it comes last.

items.statement: Twenty-two players are on the field at the same time.
items.explanation: True. Two teams of eleven are on the field at a time — you have to do the arithmetic.

items.statement: More than a third of the league's teams reach the playoffs.
items.explanation: True. Fourteen of the 32 teams qualify, which is nearly half.

items.statement: You score a field goal by carrying the ball into the end zone.
items.explanation: False. That is a touchdown. A field goal is kicked between the uprights.

items.statement: No player has won the Super Bowl more times than Tom Brady.
items.explanation: True. The text says he “won more Super Bowls than any other player”.

items.statement: Lawrence Taylor's job was to defend, not to throw the ball.
items.explanation: True. He was a linebacker, a defensive position; the quarterback is the one who throws.

exercises.title: Vocabulary in Use
exercises.instructions: Choose the word or phrase that fits the meaning.

items.prompt: A week in the season when a team does not play is called a ___.
items.explanation: A bye week is a scheduled week off.

items.prompt: When a losing team recovers and wins, we call it a ___.
items.explanation: A comeback is a recovery from a losing position — as in Super Bowl LI.

items.prompt: A long-running competition between two teams is a ___.
items.explanation: A rivalry is an ongoing competition between the same two teams or people.

items.prompt: If the other team ___, they take control of the ball.
items.explanation: To take over is to take control of something from someone else.

items.prompt: The area where a team scores a touchdown is the ___.
items.explanation: The end zone is the scoring area at each end of the field.

exercises.title: Complete the Summary
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct word for each blank.

items.explanation: The two conferences are the NFC and the AFC.
items.prompt: The NFL has 32 teams, divided into two ___.

items.explanation: A touchdown means reaching the opponent's end zone.
items.prompt: A team scores a touchdown by getting the ball into the opponent's ___.

items.explanation: The game went to overtime, which is extra time played when the score is level.
items.prompt: In Super Bowl LI the Patriots won in ___ after trailing by 25 points.

items.explanation: A receiver catches passes; a linebacker defends and a quarterback throws.
items.prompt: Jerry Rice was a wide ___ who caught more passes than anyone in NFL history.

items.explanation: To read a defense means to understand what the other team is about to do.
items.prompt: Peyton Manning was known for ___ a defense almost like a coach.

discussion: Is there one sport in your country that works the way the NFL does in the United States — something people organize their weekend around? Describe it.
The text says you do not have to follow the NFL closely to notice it. Is there something like that where you live?
American football has complicated rules. Explain the rules of a sport you know well to someone who has never seen it, in about five sentences.
Fans still argue about who the greatest player was. Why do you think people enjoy arguments that cannot be settled?
